vc_tomography · how a scan type is calibrated and reconstructed

BM18 mosaic: calibration and filtered backprojection

Helical scans of one sample at different places on the rotation stage (tiles), for a sample much wider than the detector. This page follows PHercParis4 at 1.129 µm on ESRF BM18 (19 tiles) from its frames to reconstructed slices: what the geometry calibration measures for each tile and between tiles, how one tile is reconstructed by filtered backprojection, and how all tiles are joined into one sinogram and reconstructed by a single filtered backprojection.

The acquisitionCommandsGeometry calibrationIntensity calibrationFiltered backprojection of one tileEach tile aloneOne FBP over all tilesWhat is measured but not applied

The acquisition

A mosaic is many helical scans (tiles) of one sample that is much wider than the detector. Between tiles the sample moves on top of the rotation stage (sx, sy); the stage under the rotation stays put. The rotation axis therefore falls on the same detector column in every tile, near the detector's edge, and each tile puts another cylinder of the sample on the axis. Each tile is a half acquisition of a disc around its own axis, and the discs of neighbouring tiles overlap.

vc_tomography reconstructs a mosaic in two ways, from one geometry calibration. Each tile alone: one disc per tile. One FBP over all tiles (whole-canvas FBP): the tiles' sinograms are joined into one before filtering. vc_tomography_calibration geometry measures what both need: each tile's own geometry from its own views, and the tiles' places against each other from comparisons between neighbouring tiles. Both methods are shown, on frames read at a quarter of the detector's resolution from a projection store, which holds 3.12 turns of every tile's helix; positions are stored (full-resolution) pixels unless a figure says otherwise.

Commands

For a mosaic there are two steps: the geometry calibration of all tiles, and the reconstruction, of one tile from Python or of all tiles as one slice. These are the commands and calls of docs/calibration.md and docs/reconstruction.md for this scan type, as they were run for this page.

The geometry calibration, of all 19 tiles at once, the centre tile first:

vc_tomography_calibration geometry T0-01.h5 T1-01.h5 ... T2-12.h5 --out geometry.json \
    --row-time-us -3.5 --reduce 2 --projections projections.zarr
  • --row-time-us -3.5: the camera's row time for this acquisition, given because no stretch on disk holds a refill (see Row time).
  • --reduce 2 --projections read the frames from the projection store at a quarter; with frames on disk as stored they are left out.
  • The first master is the reference tile: its rotation axis is the origin of the tiles' places.

Each tile alone, from Python:

from vc_tomography import mosaic
rec, info = mosaic.tile_reconstructor(master, open('geometry.json').read(), 'T0-01',
                                      reduce=2, projections='projections.zarr/T0-01')
slices = rec.reconstruct(456, 457)      # FBP, ramp filter only
  • Every tile was given the centre tile's row_origin plus its own calibrated height, so that one slice number is one height of the sample in all tiles.

One FBP over all tiles. vc_tomography_reconstruct takes a mosaic when the geometry calibration it is given is of a mosaic's tiles; from Python it is mosaic.canvas_reconstruction:

vc_tomography_reconstruct RAW_DATA --projection_store projections.zarr --reduce 2 \
    --set geometry=geometry.json --fractions 0.5 --keep_tiles --tag canvas_fbp_default
r = mosaic.canvas_reconstruction('RAW_DATA', 'geometry.json', reduce=2,
                                 projection_store='projections.zarr', keep_tiles=True)
slices = r.reconstruct(453, 454)        # (1, 9005, 9005) float32, 1 / cm
  • --keep_tiles keeps every tile's reconstructor alive between chunks. It saves setting each tile up again and costs device memory, which a quarter-resolution run has to spare.

Geometry calibration

To put a raw pixel value on the line through the sample that it measured, the reconstruction must know, for every frame of every scan, which ray each detector pixel recorded. The geometry calibration measures this from the scans' own frames and writes it to one file, geometry.json.

The model

A ray through the sample is named by the angle θ it is seen at, its distance s from the sample's origin across the beam (pixels) and its height z (rows). A stored pixel (c, v) looks along the ideal position (X, Y) = (c + Eu, v + Ev), where Eu(c, v) and Ev(c, v) are the detector map (lens distortion). Scan k records the ray at

X = axisk + axis_slopek·(H − Hmid,k) + A(2θ) + u + roll·(Y − middle row)
Y = z + heightk + (1 + axial_scalek)·H + B(θ) − roll·u
u = s + dk·(cos θ, sin θ)

θ and H are the angle and height that the master records, taken at the time the pixel's row was exposed: row v of frame f at the time of frame f + row_time·(v − middle row). The unknowns are:

  • axis, axis_slope: the rotation axis' column in the scan, and its drift per row of travel along the axis;
  • axial_scale: the sample really travels (1 + axial_scale) rows per row of recorded travel (the helical pitch);
  • height, d: a tile's height and place on the rotation stage against the centre tile (the anchor, where both are zero). A tile's own views do not measure them; the comparisons between neighbouring tiles do;
  • roll: the rotation of the detector's columns against the rotation axis;
  • A, B: what the rotation stage does within a turn, shared by all scans: the axis column twice per turn and the sample's height once per turn;
  • Eu, Ev: the detector map. For a mosaic only its four terms of a radial displacement about the detector's middle are solved: the tiles' comparisons do not tell a general map from the roll;
  • height_once: per tile, the height once per turn that its own opposite views show beyond the stage's. A rotation axis that leans towards the beam produces it for any tile that is off the stage's centre;
  • column_scale: per tile, the scale of its image across the beam against the centre tile's (u·(1 + column_scale) in place of u);
  • pitch: the lean of the rotation axis towards the beam. Two tiles at equal angle record the same rays pitch × their distance along the beam rows apart. It is measured and reported, not applied.

The last solve of this acquisition has 82 free unknowns for 115 535 patch matches. Each solve is one least-squares problem (Ceres), with a Huber loss of 0.03 px on each match so that a wrong match cannot pull the solution. No match has an offset of its own: what the model cannot explain stays in the residuals.

Layout

The step first reads what it can without registering anything precisely: the frames on disk, the frames per turn, the rows that hold something across the whole width (the sample mount, kept out of every comparison), the direction of the detector's rows against the stage's travel, and a coarse rotation axis per scan. A scan with the axis in its field gets the axis from profiles of frames half a turn apart; a scan without it is placed against its neighbour by profiles at equal frames. The log below is at a quarter, so its columns are quarter pixels.

Row time

The detectors read their rows one after another while the sample turns (a rolling shutter), so each row of a frame belongs to a slightly different angle, and in a helix to a slightly different height. The calibration needs the time between two rows.

No refill falls in the frames on disk, so the value is given: -3.50 µs per stored row (-0.56 of a frame period over the 2 368 rows; the last row is read first). It was measured on this acquisition from the tiles at equal angle: the column offset between two tiles belongs to the angle at which each row was exposed, so a row time shears it along the rows. Ignored, the row time turns each frame slightly between its first and last row: by 0.9 to 1.6 px at the edge of a tile's field.

Comparisons

Fine measurements come from registering blocks of frames that recorded the same lines through the sample on different parts of the detector. A block is 32 frames by up to 512 columns; it is cut into patches of 128 × 128 stored pixels, and each patch is registered to a fraction of a pixel in frames, rows and columns (band-passed phase correlation, repeated until no displacement is left). A patch is accepted with a correlation above 0.3.

  • Opposite views: a stretch against itself half a turn on, mirrored about the coarse axis column. They exist only where the axis lies inside the field, in the strip of columns that is seen from both sides. 19 098 patches.
  • Two tiles at equal angle: two neighbouring tiles record the same rays at one angle on columns that differ by (dk − dj)·(cos θ, sin θ). That offset swings by the tiles' distance over a turn, so both detectors hold such rays only near the two angles at which the tiles line up along the beam. 64 330 patches.
  • Two tiles half a turn apart: the second tile half a turn on, mirrored. With the axis near the detector's edge both detectors hold such rays over the half of the turn in which the second tile lies on the first's far side. Their rows are not fitted (they differ by twice the pitch times the depth); their columns are. 32 107 patches.

The comparisons between tiles are planned from where the tiles are. The stage positions in the masters (sx, sy) give that to a few tens of pixels, but the record does not say how the motors' plane lies in the model's. The step measures a few blocks between the centre tile and its six neighbours under each of the eight possible orientations and takes the one whose blocks register: here 960 patches are accepted under d = (v, −u), against 323 under the next best. It then compares all 42 pairs of neighbouring tiles (tiles whose discs overlap), each block registered whole before its patches so that the motors' error is taken up.

  the motors' plane in the model's: of the eight orientations the patches accepted between the anchor and its neighbours are 960, 4, 3, 323, 1, 4, 9, 5; taken: d = (v, -u) of…
  the tiles with each other: 42 pairs of neighbours, 12096 blocks planned, 96437 patches of 32 accepted (64330 at equal angle, 32107 half a turn apart) in 161 s (reading 20, …
  three solves: all together (157 unknowns), each tile's own parameters from its own views, the shared terms and the places with a scale per tile (82 unknowns); the tiles lie…

Solve

For a mosaic the step solves three times.

  1. All together. Every unknown from all comparisons, with the detector map's four radial terms free (157 unknowns).
  2. Each tile's own parameters again (axis column, axis slope, axial scale, height once per turn), from its own views only, with the places, roll, stage motion and map of the first solve held. In the first solve the 96 437 matches between tiles outnumber a tile's own 1 005 and pull its axis column off where its own views put it.
  3. The shared terms and the places again (places, heights, roll, pitch, stage motion, map), from all comparisons, with the tiles' own parameters held and one more unknown per tile: the scale of its image across the beam (82 unknowns).
Root mean square of what is left of the patch matches [stored px], under 3 sets of parameters applied to the same matches: the coarse layout alone (coarse axis columns, the tiles at the motors' places, nothing solved), the model solved without a detector map, and the calibration's model. The rows of two tiles half a turn apart are not fitted.

The tiles lie up to 42 px from where the motors put them. Over the 19 tiles the axis column spreads by 0.66 px (0.17 rms) about 4106.50, and the axial scale by 100 ppm about -1454 ppm. Shared by all tiles: roll -127.0 µrad; the stage lifts the sample by 0.28 rows once per turn and moves the axis by 0.27 px twice per turn. The tiles at equal angle give the lean of the rotation axis towards the beam: -58.6 µrad. The tiles' own views show the same lean: their height once per turn is 0.23 to 0.33 rows in the first ring and 0.39 to 0.80 in the second, growing with the tile's distance from the centre. A calibration at a quarter carries a small common offset against one at full resolution (axis columns about 0.2 px lower, axial scales about 200 ppm lower).

Intensity calibration

A mosaic has no merged frame, so there is no separate intensity step. The tile reconstructor reduces each tile's own darks and flats when it is made: the mean of the 400 darks, and the mean of each of the two series of 401 flats, every flat frame first scaled to the nominal ring current of 0.2 A (dark + (flat − dark)·0.2 / I). A projection is divided by the flat interpolated between the two series and by its own ring current. From a projection store these images are the store's, taken through the same low-pass as the frames.

Each tile's weight map is formed from its flats (the smoothed mean flat over its maximum, with a taper at the detector's top and bottom), with a taper at the detector's far edge and a slope across the rotation axis, as for an HA scan. Nothing in it knows yet that every ray also crosses sample outside the tile's disc.

Filtered backprojection of one tile

The default method is filtered backprojection (backprojector=fbp) with no projection filter. It reconstructs a chunk of slices in the stages below; every stage has a CPU and a CUDA implementation with the same results. For a mosaic the same pipeline runs on one tile, with one scan in the frame. The whole-canvas FBP further down uses stages 1 to 6 of it for every tile and replaces the rest.

  1. Read. For each scan, the projections that see the chunk's slices and, of each, only the detector rows the slices fall on, plus the context rows of the kernels.
  2. Flat-field. Each raw sample becomes a transmission: (raw − dark) / (flat − dark), with the flat interpolated between the series and the projection scaled by its ring current.
  3. Grid. Each projection is read at the pose the geometry calibration gives it. Along the axis, the slice lies at a fractional detector row, read with a 16-row Lanczos kernel (z_interp=lanczos8) through the detector map's row displacement. Across the beam, each row is resampled exactly (a band-limited, non-uniform Fourier resampling, x_interp=sinc) onto the ideal columns at the scan's fractional offset. The value times its weight, and the weight, are added into the sinogram row of the projection's angle.
  4. Match brightness. Each scan after the first is matched to the scans before it in a 25 × 25 px window at their seam (luminosity_repartition). Not applicable to one tile.
  5. Divide and mend. The sums are divided by the summed weights, which gives the weighted mean transmission of every ray. Columns without weight take the nearest measured value.
  6. Filter, then −log. Projection filters (Paganin phase retrieval, unsharp mask, ...) act here; the default chain is empty. Then the transmission becomes a line integral, −ln, clipped to [10⁻⁶, 10].
  7. Balance. A line through the sample may be recorded twice, from opposite sides. Each recording gets the weight W / (W + W of the opposite view, mirrored about the axis), so that every line counts once.
  8. Ramp filter. Each sinogram row is filtered with the Ram-Lak ramp (filter_name=ramlak). The row is padded with its opposite view, mirrored about the axis, so the filter does not see a cut where a scan's field ends.
  9. Backproject. Each filtered row, times its balanced weight, is smeared back across the slice along its rays: the backprojector is exact and pixel-driven, the rows upsampled twice (FFT) and interpolated with a cubic B-spline (fbp(interp=bspline3, oversample=2)). Values are scaled to linear attenuation in cm⁻¹.

Details that depend on the calibration:

  • One sinogram row per view (angle_interp=views). The sinogram of this slice has 10 278 rows on an angular grid of 10 000 bins per turn: a slice is seen for more than one turn where the detector is taller than the travel per turn, and two views a turn apart are not at exactly the same angle. Each is filtered and backprojected at its own measured angle with its share of the weight.
  • Row time. A slice lies on another detector row in every projection, so the angle of each sinogram row is corrected per slice by the row time (−0.56 of a frame period from the first row to the last).
  • Beam divergence. The BM18 source is far away: the rays turn by 6 nrad per stored column, which the backprojector follows in the slice.

Each tile alone

Each tile reconstructs a disc of radius 4 110 px around its own axis. Because the sample is wider than any tile, the ramp filter sees projections that are cut at the frame's edge with sample on both sides: a lone tile's slice carries a slow shading (an offset and a bowl across the disc) that cannot be removed from the tile's data alone. Edges and fine detail are not affected.

One FBP over all tiles

A tile reconstructed alone ramp-filters rows that end inside the sample. The ramp filter is not local (its kernel falls as one over the distance squared), so what lies beyond a row's end is missing from every filtered value: each tile's slice gets a slow shading, and neighbouring tiles disagree where they overlap. The whole-canvas FBP avoids this by joining the tiles' rows before the filter. The mosaic then is one sample with one sinogram.

The canvas is the slice of the whole mosaic: 9 005 × 9 005 pixels of 4.516 µm here (36 020 at full resolution), with the centre tile's rotation axis at its middle pixel. A tile's place on it, (ax, ay), is where its rotation axis passes through the canvas; it follows from the calibration's place d of the sample on the rotation stage as (−d0, d1).

  1. Each tile's rows. Every tile runs stages 1 to 6 of its own pipeline (read, flat-field, grid through its detector map and row time, projection filters, −log) and hands over, per slice, one row per angular bin of the turn with the weights the values were measured with. Nothing is balanced or filtered yet.
  2. Place. At the angle a, column c of a tile's row records the canvas column c − rot_center + half + ax cos a + ay sin a: over a turn the tile's rows swing across the canvas by the tile's distance from the centre. Each row is delayed by the fraction of that offset exactly (a band-limited shift) and added at the whole column: value times weight into one sum, weight into another. A tile's weight falls to nothing over the last 200 stored columns at either end of its rows.
  3. Levels. Tiles recorded hours apart differ by a small level in their line integrals. One additive level per tile and slice is solved by least squares from the rays that two tiles both recorded at the same angle, with the centre tile's level held at zero.
  4. Fold. The ray at angle a and canvas column t is the ray at a + 180° and column −t. The two halves of the turn are summed onto each other, and the sums divided: every ray becomes the weighted mean of all its recordings, by any tile from either side. A ray that no tile recorded takes the nearest recorded value of its row.
  5. One ramp filter, one backprojection. The rows are now whole, 9 005 columns wide. The half turn of 5 000 rows is ramp-filtered and backprojected once onto the whole canvas with the same kernels as any other scan (Ram-Lak ramp, exact backprojector with cubic B-spline rows upsampled twice). Pixels outside every tile's disc are set to zero.

The whole-canvas slice is the same whatever the chunking: reconstructing this slice alone or as the first of two gives identical values. With the documented filter chain the same command takes --set "filters=paganin(delta_beta=1000)+unsharp(sigma=1.2,coeff=4)"; the filters act in each tile's pipeline, before the rows are joined.

What is measured but not applied

  • Slices are reconstructed one at a time in a two-dimensional model. Anything that moves a ray out of its slice is not applied: the beam's divergence along the axis, and a tilt of the rotation axis towards the beam.
  • The tiles' rotations against each other are not solved, and the detector map holds only its radial terms.
  • The lean of the rotation axis towards the beam (-59 µrad) is measured and written to the file, not applied.
  • Calibrated at a quarter, the result carries a small offset common to the tiles against a full-resolution calibration.
  • The whole-canvas FBP leaves out the beam's divergence (a tile's own slice follows it) and the tiles' rotations against each other, and it takes the tiles' angles of one angular bin as equal: on this slice they differ by up to 0.19 of a bin, which is 2.2 stored px along the tangent at the canvas' edge.
  • A tile's own slice carries slow shading from the sample outside its disc; the whole-canvas slice does not.
